analysis.one_liner: Raises the top corporate tax rate back to 35% and closes offshore tax loopholes used by multinationals.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo several tax advantages that large and multinational corporations have held since 2017. It would bring back graduated corporate rates topping out at 35% on income over $10 million, tax the foreign profits of U.S.-managed companies, tighten rules against corporate inversions and tax-haven structures, and require multinational companies to report revenues, profits, and employees country by country. It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and not a single other member of the House signed on.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit if the bill's provisions raise federal revenue from large corporations, which reduces pressure to cut services or raise other taxes. Domestic-focused companies that already pay full U.S. rates would also face less disadvantage against multinationals that shift profits offshore.

how_it_helps.text: Restores graduated corporate tax rates reaching 35% on taxable income above $10 million, reversing the flat 21% rate that has applied since 2018 [S3].

Taxes all income of controlled foreign corporations so that foreign subsidiaries cannot escape U.S. tax by parking profits abroad, and repeals the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income, a 2017 break for companies earning profits booked offshore [S3].

Tightens anti-inversion rules so that companies that move their legal headquarters abroad but keep majority U.S. ownership are still taxed as domestic corporations, and treats foreign corporations managed and controlled in the U.S. with $50 million or more in assets as U.S. taxpayers [S3].

Repeals the 'check-the-box' rules that let companies create or erase foreign subsidiaries on paper to dodge taxes, expands the base erosion and anti-abuse tax down to companies with $25 million in gross receipts, and requires country-by-country disclosure of revenues, profits, and employees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations — especially multinationals with offshore subsidiaries, companies that have inverted, and firms with big foreign-derived income — would pay substantially more tax, and their shareholders would bear that cost through lower after-tax returns.

drawbacks.text: Raising the top corporate rate to 35% and taxing all foreign income unilaterally would put U.S.-headquartered multinationals at a steep disadvantage against foreign competitors taxed at much lower rates, which could encourage companies to redouble relocation efforts or shift real operations abroad [S3].

The bill layers many new regimes on at once — graduated rates, full taxation of subpart F income, country-by-country credit limits, interest caps, and treaty overrides — creating significant compliance costs and administrative complexity for both companies and the IRS [S3].
Personal service corporations would face a flat 35% rate with no graduated rates, a sharp increase for professional firms organized as corporations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real and well-documented avoidance channels — inversions, check-the-box hybrids, profit shifting to tax havens — and would raise substantial revenue from corporations rather than individuals. The main honest objection is design: raising the rate to 35% while the rest of the world sits far lower, without coordination, risks pushing more companies and jobs offshore unless paired with international agreements, and the bill's complexity would be a genuine burden. Its fatal practical weakness was political: it never attracted a single cosponsor.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or markup, until the 117th Congress ended, and no other member of the House signed on to it.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Corporate Tax Dodging Prevention Act on March 26, 2021 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor count remained zero throughout [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations and their shareholders, who kept the flat 21% corporate rate, the foreign-derived intangible income deduction, and the offshore planning structures the bill would have shut down. The Ways and Means Committee's decision not to act was decisive; no member of either party pressed to move it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinational corporations kept their tax breaks

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no Republican ever took a position on the bill on the record; notably, not a single one of the 222 House Democrats cosponsored it either [S4].

industries.note: The bill's core provisions — full taxation of foreign subsidiary income, treaty-benefit limits, base-erosion tax expansion, and repeal of the foreign intangible income deduction — are all aimed at structures multinationals use to keep profits out of U.S. tax. Those structures cost the treasury revenue that otherwise reduces the burden on individual taxpayers.

The bill would limit foreign tax credits for 'dual capacity' payments to countries that levy a fee and grant the company a special economic benefit in return, a break these extractive industries rely on when operating abroad.

Repealing the foreign-derived intangible income deduction removes a reduced tax rate on income from U.S.-owned intellectual property sold to foreign markets, a benefit that flows disproportionately to patent-rich drug and tech firms.

industries.industry: Corporate tax advisory and accounting industry
industries.note: Repealing check-the-box elections, tightening inversion rules, and requiring country-by-country reporting would shrink the market for the cross-border structuring work this industry sells to large clients.
